_comment: One war told as a book of episodes (campaign.md in this folder's parent). Each season is one story folder, scouted, planned, written and finished like any episode; the book reads them in order. The seasons' `when`, `edge`, `pivotal`, `aliases` and `start` are LEADS, as in candidates.json: never facts and never a ranking. A scout establishes each from fetched sources and the edge re-check tries to refute it. The working title and subtitle are the author's to change; the question is proposed by the scout's outline.
title: Hannibal's War
subtitle: Rome against Carthage, 218 to 201 BC, from the record
author: Lawrence, 2026-10-30, after Caesar in Gaul was published: "Yes you can move on to hanibal : GO" (the recommendation: the Second Punic War as the second campaign book, the landed Siege of Syracuse as one of its seasons).
_question: Proposed by the scout's outline as one short line in the author's voice (16 words at most), written here only when he has approved it (campaign.md §4).

sources: Polybius, The Histories, Shuckburgh translation (1889): book III whole; books VII to XI and XIV to XV in part (syracuse-213bc fetched volume 1 as s1)
Livy, The History of Rome, Roberts translation: books XXI to XXX (syracuse-213bc fetched Books 9 to 26 as s3; Books 27 to 36 are a second volume)
mainAccounts.note: LEAD: no commander's own account survives. Silenus and Sosylus, the Greeks who wrote Hannibal's campaigns from his camp, are lost. Polybius is the main account, Livy beside him. By his own account Polybius questioned men who had been there and went over the Alps himself to learn the route. No season is marked `ownWords` unless its scout finds a participant's own words quoted at length (a letter, a speech a source says it copies), so the seasons are told without an immersive (L1) passage unless one is found (campaign.md §2).

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 219–218 BC: Saguntum and the Alps
seasons.edge: Logistic: an army with elephants taken from Spain to Italy overland; the elephants ferried over the Rhone on earth-covered rafts; the Alps crossed late in the year at a cost in men and animals the sources count
seasons.pivotal: The war came to Italy instead of Spain or Africa, where Rome had planned to fight it
start: gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book III (Shuckburgh, 1889)
gutenberg: Livy, book XXI (Roberts)
wikipedia: Siege of Saguntum; Hannibal's crossing of the Alps (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 218–217 BC: the Trebia and Lake Trasimene
seasons.edge: Tactical: a force hidden in a stream bed at the Trebia, and a Roman army drawn across a winter river before it had eaten; at Trasimene an army caught on the march between hills and the lake
seasons.pivotal: Two Roman armies lost in two years; Rome turned to a dictator
start: gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book III (Shuckburgh, 1889)
gutenberg: Livy, books XXI and XXII (Roberts)
wikipedia: Battle of the Trebia; Battle of Lake Trasimene (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 217 BC: Fabius and the war of delay
seasons.edge: Logistic: a Roman general who shadowed the invader on high ground and would not give battle; the invader's night escape from the Falernian plain behind cattle with burning faggots tied to their horns
seasons.pivotal: Delay as a way of war, mocked at the time, became Rome's way of fighting Hannibal after Cannae
start: gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book III (Shuckburgh, 1889)
gutenberg: Livy, book XXII (Roberts)
gutenberg: Plutarch, Life of Fabius (Dryden, rev. Clough)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 216 BC: Cannae
seasons.edge: Tactical: Hannibal's double envelopment of a much larger Roman army: a centre that bowed back, African infantry on the wings, cavalry closing the rear
seasons.pivotal: Rome's worst defeat; several Italian allies went over to Carthage (candidates.json cannae-216bc)
start: gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book III (Shuckburgh, 1889)
gutenberg: Livy, book XXII (Roberts)
gutenberg: Plutarch, Life of Fabius (Dryden, rev. Clough)
wikipedia: Battle of Cannae (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 216–211 BC: Capua and the march on Rome
seasons.edge: Logistic: Rome's manpower and its refusal to ransom its captives or to treat; siege lines round Capua held while Hannibal marched on Rome to draw them off
seasons.pivotal: After Cannae the war did not end: Capua went over to Hannibal and was retaken, and his march on Rome did not raise the siege
start: gutenberg: Livy, books XXIII to XXVI (Roberts)
gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book IX (Shuckburgh, 1889), the march on Rome
gutenberg: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus (Dryden, rev. Clough)

seasons.subject: The Siege of Syracuse
seasons._landed: Landed in StoryMaker 2026-10-19 in the first voice (v1); not published. Not scouted again: its dossier's people and peoples are the cast lines the other seasons reuse (campaign.md §2). The outline proposes whether it is told again in voice v2 for the book, as Alesia was (project.json `tellingOf`); the author decides.

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 211–206 BC: Scipio in Spain
seasons.edge: Tactical: New Carthage taken by men who waded its lagoon at the ebb, a tide the attacker had learned of before he marched; at Ilipa the usual order of battle reversed
seasons.pivotal: Carthage lost Spain, its silver and the recruits that fed Hannibal's army
start: gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, books X and XI (Shuckburgh, 1889)
gutenberg: Livy, books XXV to XXVIII (Roberts)
internet-archive: Appian, The Spanish Wars (Horace White, 1912)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 207 BC: the Metaurus
seasons.edge: Logistic: dispatch riders taken on the road; a Roman consul's secret forced march north with picked men to join his colleague before the second Carthaginian army could reach Hannibal
seasons.pivotal: Hannibal's brother and his army were destroyed, and no reinforcement reached Hannibal in Italy
start: gutenberg: Livy, book XXVII (Roberts)
gutenberg: Polybius, Histories, book XI (Shuckburgh, 1889)
wikipedia: Battle of the Metaurus (leads and references only)

seasons.subject: Hannibal's War, 204–202 BC: Africa and Zama
seasons.edge: Tactical: winter camps of reed huts burned in one night; at Zama lanes left open through the Roman lines for the elephants to run down, and Numidian cavalry that had changed sides
seasons.pivotal: Carthage asked for peace; the war's end made Rome the power of the western Mediterranean
